# PREFACE

**ALBRECHT DIETERICH** had the members of the Heidelberg advanced seminar study "selected pieces from Greek papyri" in the summer of 1905. Under this pseudonym, the Greek magical papyri appeared in the course catalog of the Ruperto-Carola <note>The Latin name for Heidelberg University</note>. For at that time, it was not yet advisable for a proper philologist <note>A scholar who studies historical languages and literary texts</note> to publicly admit to engaging with such "low-level" products of uneducated social classes—products of blatant superstition that did not merit the name "literature." In specific exceptional cases, where the use of magical papyri and lead curse tablets <term>defixiones: lead tablets inscribed with curses or spells, often buried to invoke underworld powers</term> was excused for higher purposes within a larger context, interaction with Abraxas and his associates <note>Abraxas is a mystical name found in Gnostic texts and on amulets, often representing a supreme deity or solar power</note> might still be tolerated. This was true even if it caused some frowning among those classically-minded scholars who, along with **FRANÇOIS LENORMANT**, smelled only "Gnostic cheese" <note>original: "fromage gnostique"; a dismissive French term used by Lenormant to describe the perceived rot or confusion of later mystical and magical syncretism</note> in all magical documents of the post-Christian era. Those who were not trapped in prejudice and sought to recognize the valuable historical and folkloric material within the disorganized mess of magical recipes and rituals were few and far between at the beginning of the century.

Leading them was **ALBRECHT DIETERICH**, who built his still-controversial *Mithras Liturgy* (1903, 1910, 1923) on a text from the Great Paris Magical Papyrus. This followed his earlier work pointing out the untapped treasures of the magical papyri in his award-winning Bonn doctoral dissertation (1888), his Habilitation thesis (1891), his work *Abraxas* (1891), his *Nekyia* (1893), and other incidental mentions. Alongside him, **RICHARD WÜNSCH** sought to keep interest in the magic tablets alive: they gained some prestige from the fact that those found in Attica could appear within the *Corpus Inscr. Att.* <note>Corpus Inscriptionum Atticarum: a major collection of ancient Greek inscriptions from the region of Athens</note> in 1897. **WÜNSCH'S** book *Sethian Curse Tablets from Rome* (1898) provided significant inspiration for the religious and cultural-historical treatment of such traditions.

**RICHARD REITZENSTEIN** also recognized their value early on; as early as 1892, he concerned himself with the reconstruction of the "Hymn to Hecate" from the Great Paris Magic Book in a penetrating study for the Rostock *Index Lectionum*, and his *Poimandres* (1904) assigned the fragmentary Papyrus Mimaut of the Louvre its important place in religious history for the first time. The theological side was represented by **ADOLF DEISSMANN**, an unbiased researcher of superstitious documents. He laid his linguistically groundbreaking— <note>The text cuts off mid-sentence; Deissmann is known for showing that New Testament Greek was the common language of the people, similar to that found in papyri.</note>

<summary>This preface describes the early 20th-century academic struggle to have Greek magical papyri recognized as legitimate objects of historical study rather than mere superstition. It credits scholars like Dieterich, Wünsch, Reitzenstein, and Deissmann for breaking through classical prejudices to explore these "untapped treasures."</summary>
<keywords>History of scholarship, Greek magical papyri, Albrecht Dieterich, Richard Wünsch, Richard Reitzenstein, Adolf Deissmann, Gnosticism, Philology, Curse tablets</keywords>

# PREFACE

...based his 'Bible Studies' (1895; 3rd English edition 1923) on a lead curse tablet from Hadrumetum and, in his widely circulated 'Light from the East' (1908, 4th edition 1923), treated the magical texts of the papyri as being without hesitation of equal value to all other late antique documents he discussed. There is no lack of other scholars of rank and reputation who, alongside **DIETERICH**, **WÜNSCH**, and **DEISSMANN**, strove for the proper evaluation of magical literature as a direct source for our knowledge of faith and superstition, language and culture, and 'folklore' in Egypt during the first centuries of the Christian era—nearly all of them have an intellectual connection with those pioneers or emerged from their school. Only a few stand alone, such as **OTTO CRUSIUS** who, influenced by **ERWIN ROHDE**, devoted the greatest interest to magical papyri in his studies of religious history and folklore, without however publishing anything substantial about them; and **AUGUSTE AUDOLLENT**, who in 1904 published his meritorious collection of Greek and Latin lead curse tablets <term>defixiones: lead tablets inscribed with curses or spells, often buried to invoke underworld powers</term>. The immediate future has already shown that **A. DIETERICH** and his fellow combatants were on the right path when they included magical literature without distinction in their philological <note>The study of language in oral and written historical sources</note> studies and advocated for them: the number of researchers who utilized magical papyri and curse tablets for their work has grown astonishingly in the last two decades; proof of this can be found in my overview of the users of papyrus texts (Archive for Papyrus Research <note>original: 'Archiv für Papyrusforschung'</note> VIII 1926, 132–165), which already requires extensive supplements.

This corpus <note>A 'corpus' is a comprehensive collection of written texts; here it refers to the 'Papyri Graecae Magicae' (PGM)</note> of Greek magical papyri also traces back to the influence and inspiration of **ALBRECHT DIETERICH**. In those Heidelberg seminar exercises of the summer of 1905 and in personal conversation, he often emphasized the main reason for their contemptuous treatment by philological and theological researchers: the lack of an easily accessible, generally readable, and understandable edition of the texts, which were published in scattered locations and sometimes very poorly edited. Seventy-three years have passed from the first treatment of these documents, provided by **CHARLES WYCLIFFE GOODWIN** for the Cambridge Antiquarian Society (1852), to the most recent, presented by **SAM. EITREM** to the Norwegian Academy of Science and Letters <note>original: 'Norske Videnskaps-Akademi'</note> in Oslo in 1925. The methods of editorial technique have changed during this period, and views and interpretations of almost all problems regarding magical papyri have constantly shifted. Thus, the first editions, when held side by side, present quite a colorful picture. **CH. W. GOODWIN** edited Papyrus XLVI of the British Museum; he followed the Greek text with an English translation and the most necessary explanations. **GUSTAV PARTHEY** proceeded similarly when he published the two Berlin specimens in 1865; he also provided the original text with a German translation, while the Dutchman **C. LEEMANS** provided a Latin translation alongside his; his 1885 edition of the two Leiden magical papyri goes back to the period before 1830 in its textual basis and

It credits Albrecht Dieterich for initiating the effort to create a standardized, accessible edition of these scattered and often ignored texts.</summary>

VII
<header>PREFACE</header>

...must therefore be considered the oldest attempt at systematically editing Greek magical texts; for the credit for the first reading and meaningful transcription of the roll and the book in the Museum of Antiquities belongs not to **LEEMANS**, but to **C. J. C. REUVENS**. The often questionable additions of the *Latin version* <note>original: 'Versio latina'</note> and commentary are **LEEMANS'** work alone. These earliest editors of magical papyri all proceeded from the view that such uncommon texts required a translation to facilitate understanding, just as **KARL OTFRIED MUELLER**—in his review of **C. J. REUVENS'** **Letter to Mr. Letronne** (Göttingen Scholarly Announcements 1831, 545–554), significant already for the refined scholar's high interest in such abstruse texts—deemed it useful to translate samples from the Leiden magical papyri into German. It would certainly have contributed to the wider dissemination of this literature, which is often textually corrupted and difficult to understand in content, had the subsequent editors remained true to the method of their predecessors. 

But the Viennese papyrologist <term>papyrologist: a scholar who studies and interprets ancient documents written on papyrus</term> **CARL WESSELY** took a different path of publication. It is his great and lasting merit to have brought to light a number of still unknown magical papyri of high significance in terms of content through two weighty publications in the *Memoirs of the Vienna Academy* <note>original: 'Denkschriften der Wiener Akademie'</note>. The Great Magical Book of the National Library of Paris <note>original: 'Bibliothèque Nationale Paris'</note>, Greek Supplement 574—a collective work of 3,274 lines on 18 double-sheets, acquired by the Imperial Library in 1857 from the Anastasi Collection, announced by **E. MILLER** in some hymnic samples without citation of sources in 1868, and by **E. REVILLOUT** in Coptic examples in 1876—this most extensive magical document was transcribed and shared in its entirety for the first time by **WESSELY** (Memoirs 36, 1888). 

In doing so, he completely renounced the production of a 'readable' text in order to give merely a transcription of the original version of the papyrus itself. Thus, he provided valuable material, which, however, certainly cannot be used by every reader without difficulty. Even the lack of accents and punctuation marks will deter many from engaging more seriously with these texts printed in such a manner. That the first collation <note>The process of comparing a new transcription against the original manuscript to ensure accuracy</note> of the papyrus could not be achieved without errors is not surprising; **WESSELY** himself sent a revision of the edition as early as 1888/89. Simultaneously with the Great Paris Papyrus, he brought to light that of the Louvre No. 2391 (Mimaut), a fragment that places far greater demands on the paleographer <term>paleographer: an expert who studies and deciphers ancient handwriting</term>; additionally, in a new independent reading, he published the London Anastasi, British Museum XLVI, which had already been edited by **GOODWIN**. 

**WESSELY** applied the same editing technique when he made known the extensive magical roll of the British Museum No. CXXI, a collective manuscript, also in the Memoirs of the Vienna Academy, Volume 42, 1893, and enriched this edition with the smaller pieces from London, CXXII–CXXIV. **WESSELY** performed highly valuable pioneering work with his distinguished editions <note>original: 'editiones palmares'</note>: for these, he retains the gratitude of all historians of religion and researchers of late antiquity...

<summary>This page traces the evolution of magical papyrus scholarship, contrasting the accessible, translated approach of Reuvens and Mueller with Carl Wessely’s rigorous but difficult raw transcriptions of major Paris and London manuscripts.</summary>
<keywords>C. J. C. Reuvens, Carl Wessely, Papyrology, Great Magical Book of Paris, British Museum, transcription methods, historical scholarship</keywords>

VIII
<header>PREFACE</header>

...[language and folklore] secured. He has provided invaluable material that remains the foundation for all research in the field of ancient magic to this day. Nevertheless, it seemed desirable and timely to unite these documents—which were published by *Wessely* and his predecessors in a scattered and inconsistent manner—into a single *Body of Magical Papyri* <note>original Latin: 'Corpus Papyrorum Magicarum'</note> that offers the user a text that is as reliable as possible and edited according to fixed principles. This plan was all the more advisable because, simultaneously with *Wessely’s* edition of the London papyri numbered 121–124, *Frederik Kenyon’s* 'Greek Papyri in the British Museum' (1893) provided the same pieces in a new <term>collation: a detailed comparison of different manuscripts to identify variations</term> independent of *Wessely’s* readings (including 'The Old Woman of Apollonius' <note>original Greek: 'Γραῦς Ἀπολλωνίου'</note> in London Papyrus 125, which was missing from *Wessely’s* work). The comparison of both transcriptions frequently revealed significant differences, which *Ulrich Wilcken* pointed out in the *Göttingen Scholarly Announcements* (1894, 727–731) while presenting his own collations. Like *Wessely’s*, *Kenyon’s* edition does not offer "finished" texts, but only transcriptions without accents or punctuation; however, it possesses the advantage of being more richly annotated, and above all: the collection of plates provides all the magical papyri of the British Museum in excellent photographic reproduction—an invaluable aid for verifying the texts, their illustrations, and signs.

Thus, by 1893, all the important magical papyri were available in publications that were able to give an impression of their content; they gathered the material but could not fulfill the requirements of a consistently usable edition. To create one, or rather to have one created, was a long-standing concern of *Albrecht Dieterich*. At first, he admittedly only thought of a new edition of the "Great Paris Book," from which he treated selected parts in his advanced seminar in Heidelberg, likely with this ulterior motive. He joyfully agreed when I declared my willingness to venture upon the edition; he himself wanted to participate by editing the hymns and metrical passages. It was intended to be a small volume in the *Teubner Library* <note>original Latin: 'Bibliotheca Teubneriana', a famous series of Greek and Latin texts</note>; the revision of the text was to be carried out with the help of photographs of the entire papyrus, which *Dieterich* had obtained from Paris at that time. This edition, with a concise <term>critical apparatus: a system of notes at the bottom of a page explaining textual variants and corrections</term>, was nearly completed when *Albrecht Dieterich* was suddenly called from this life by death on May 6, 1908, shortly after he had reviewed the manuscript and promised the hymns in the near future. However, my deep involvement with the entire mass of magical papyri had already convinced me by then of the necessity for a new complete edition of these documents. When it emerged that *Ludwig Fahz*, a student of *Albrecht Dieterich* from Giessen, and *Adam Abt*, a student of *Richard Wünsch*, were at work editing the Mimaut Papyrus in the Louvre and the two Berlin papyri, a merger with them—mediated by *R. Wünsch*—seemed only beneficial to the larger plan. The technical...

IX
->**PREFACE**<-

The leadership and organization of the project were taken over by R. Wünsch, who also promised to handle the <term>metrical texts: passages written in poetic meter rather than prose</term> <note>original: "Metrica"</note> that Dieterich had not yet begun. He had several of these treated as "Divine Hymns" in the Königsberg philological seminar of 1909/10—Bruno Kusters' dissertation, "On Three Poems of the Paris Magical Papyrus" <note>original Latin: "De tribus carminibus papyri parisinae magicae"</note> (Königsberg 1911), arose from these exercises. The previously mentioned texts were assigned to Abt and Fahz, while I myself took on all the others; in addition to the large magical formulas, this included the smaller pieces of applied magic scattered throughout various collections. Georg Möller was recruited to handle the Coptic sections, which present particular difficulties for <term>Coptologists: scholars who study the Coptic language, the final stage of the ancient Egyptian language</term>, and for which Adolf Erman has performed distinguished work.

To make the texts accessible even to those who do not know Greek and Coptic, R. Wünsch and the publisher B. G. Teubner planned to include a German translation. After consulting Franz Boll, Otto Crusius, Hermann Diels, Georg Wissowa, and others, it was decided to change the <term>critical apparatus: the technical notes documenting manuscript variations</term>—originally intended for the Teubner Library series in Latin—into a German version of the briefest possible form. Thus, the core of the manuscript was with R. Wünsch in 1913, and the portion containing Papyri I–IV was almost entirely set in <term>galley proofs: preliminary printed versions used for correction</term> by the B. G. Teubner printing house when the war broke out, casting doubt on the project's continuation for many years. The war took Richard Wünsch from us; he fell in battle on May 17, 1918, in the East <note>The Eastern Front of World War I.</note>; Adam Abt died in 1918, and Georg Möller was unexpectedly snatched away from us on a journey abroad not long after. Adolf Jacoby in Luxembourg took his place, undertaking the revision of the <term>Coptic materials: texts written in the Coptic language</term> <note>original: "Coptica"</note> and the linguistic examination of many <term>magical words: the 'voces magicae' or strings of power-words common in ancient spells</term> <note>original: "Zauberworte"</note>. The edition, which continued under my leadership, also gained a welcome and expert collaborator in Sam Eitrem of Oslo. Through his annotated edition of the extensive magical papyrus of Oslo, he has proven himself an outstanding expert in Greco-Egyptian magic; he will provide Papyri Nos. 136–139 <note>original Roman numerals: CXXXVI—CXXXIX</note> and No. 3 for the collective edition, which is intended to contain the following papyri known to date:

I. Berlin, State Museums 5025

# XI

->**Preface**<-

generally until the complete appearance of the collected edition, it should be regarded as its bibliographic supplement (cf. there p. 166f.). The conclusion of the collection is intended to be formed by the metrical arrangement of the hymnic pieces and a comprehensive index.

If the edition of the <term>PGM<gloss>Papyri Graecae Magicae, or "Greek Magical Papyri," the standard collection of magical spells from Greco-Roman Egypt</gloss></term> can now appear at least in its first section (three are planned), it is primarily thanks to the generosity of the publisher **B. G. TEUBNER**. Even in the most difficult economic times <note>original: "schwierigster Zeitlage," likely referring to the hyperinflation and economic instability in Germany during the 1920s</note>, the publisher could not bring themselves to hand the work over to foreign firms. Ultimately, despite certain concerns, they did not shy away from the costs involved in resuming the printing that had begun in 1914: research in the field of Greco-Egyptian magic and the productive use of previously published magical papyri had progressed so substantially over the last decade that a complete reworking of the standing type <note>In traditional letterpress printing, "standing type" refers to the composed metal blocks held for future printing</note> (Papyri I–IV) seemed indispensable if the results of numerous studies were to be utilized and recorded within it. Wherever possible, their utilization was considered; however, by no means could every single contribution mentioned in my bibliography of magical papyri (pp. 132–165) be incorporated into the text and critical apparatus.

The revision of Papyri I–III also presented no small difficulty. A second new comparison of the Berlin scrolls yielded different results here and there than those achieved by **AD. ABT**, and the repeated checking of several columns of the **Papyrus Mimaut** with the help of good photographs—which I owe to the kindness of **CHARLES BOREUX** (Paris)—showed that the first readings of this poorly preserved, large, and important fragment by **C. WESSELY**, **L. FAHZ**, and **S. EITREM** could still not offer an absolutely reliable foundation for an edition. Even the joint collations <note>A collation is a direct comparison of a transcription against the original manuscript to ensure accuracy</note> by L. FAHZ and myself (1908) were conducted too much under the sign of haste to be considered finalized. Thus, in October–November 1927, I examined all columns of the **Pap. MIMAUT** in the Louvre once more, as thoroughly as the time and light of the season allowed. The results of this work necessitated further interventions on many pages of the already paginated text; new readings were obtained, and earlier doubtful ones had to be confirmed or denied. Of the numerous small fragments belonging to the large piece—already known to **THÉODULE DEVÉRIA**—which were kept in several envelopes alongside the new columns, several previously unrecognized words and letters were again assigned to their proper place. One of these fragments, which forms the beginning of a new column (XXII) of the great roll, provided the infallible, visible proof that **P III** did not conclude with the poorly transmitted section lines 690–732, but instead found a lost continuation—unknown to us in content and length—written by a new, beautiful hand. That the smaller fragments II and III (lines 187–494), which were inserted by L. FAHZ into the context of the text of the great roll between its <term>Recto<gloss>the front side of a papyrus sheet, where the fibers run horizontally</gloss></term> and <term>Verso<gloss>the back side of a papyrus sheet, where the fibers run vertically</gloss></term>...

# XII

->**Preface**<-

whether they actually belong here may be doubted, as has already been suggested by S. EITREM in <italic>The Greek Magical Papyri of Paris</italic> (1923), 22. The labeling of all newly identified fragments within the text was omitted; a later editor will hopefully succeed in correctly placing all existing scraps, provided they can allow themselves the necessary leisure for it. However, a significant material gain for the structure of the text is unlikely to be achieved through such effort.

The entire undertaking has enjoyed much active participation since its inception. The **PRUSSIAN ACADEMY of Sciences** supported A. ABT and L. FAHZ with grants for travel to Berlin and Paris; the **BADEN MINISTRY** for Culture and Education enabled me to undertake extended stays in London, Paris, and Berlin; the <term>Emergency Association of German Science<gloss>The "Notgemeinschaft der deutschen Wissenschaft," an organization founded after WWI to support German research during the economic crisis</gloss></term> provided a sum for the printing of the work and granted me the funds for a final study of the <term>Papyrus Mimaut<gloss>A major 3rd-century CE magical codex now held in the Louvre</gloss></term> in the Louvre: to all these authorities and institutes, due thanks for their promotion and help is expressed here on behalf of the editor, collaborators, and the publisher. If, finally, the directors of all the institutes that safeguard magical papyri met us with the greatest readiness, it was a boost for the success of the <term>collation<gloss>the process of comparing the transcribed text against the original manuscript to ensure accuracy</gloss></term> work from the very beginning. **HENRI OMONT** remained invariably kind in allowing me to study the Great Magical Book <note>original: "Großen Zauberbuchs," referring to PGM IV, the largest of the Paris magical papyri</note> of the National Library in Paris both before and after the war, just as **CHARLES BOREUX** repeatedly enabled unrestricted work on the 'Mimaut.' The days in the Louvre with **ABBÉ DRIOTON** remain as unforgettable to me as those with friends **HOLWERDA** and **BOESER** in the Leiden Museum of Antiquities. **Sir FREDERIK KENYON** most kindly granted access to the magical texts of the British Museum in London; **MEDEA NORSA**, the papyrological assistant to **GIROLAMO VITELLI** in Florence, entrusted me with the small fragment from **BRECCIA’S** last excavation on my way home from a trip to Rome in 1928, just as **OTTO GLAUNING** lent the two fragments from the Leipzig University Library to Karlsruhe for a long term. **WILHELM SCHUBART’S** friendship, however, has become the most beautiful gain of my working time in the Papyrus Institute of the State Museums in Berlin. In Karlsruhe itself, colleagues at the **BADEN STATE LIBRARY** facilitated the work in various ways, and **THEODOR LÄNGIN** understandingly gave me the opportunity for necessary study trips. To all of them, who became promoters and patrons of the undertaking, thanks are given for their assistance.

Karlsruhe, Easter 1928 —————————————————— **KARL PREISENDANZ**

## Greek Magical Papyri

Berlin, P 5025 A and B of the State Museums. Acquired in 1857 by <note>Karl Richard Lepsius (1810–1884), a pioneering Prussian Egyptologist.</note> Lepsius from the <note>Giovanni Anastasi (1780–1860) was a merchant and prolific collector of Egyptian antiquities whose collection forms the core of many European museums.</note> Anastasi collection in Paris.¹) A complete papyrus roll (total length approximately 80.2 cm with a height of 33.5 cm), inscribed in 5 columns²), divided into two parts (A and B) by a clean cut after Column 2; noted as 'broken into two parts' <note>original: "brisé en deux parties"</note> as early as Fr. The few marginal notes probably come from the same hand.⁴) The main content consists of three related magical procedures for obtaining a <term>familiar spirit<gloss>original Latin: "spiritus familiaris"; a supernatural entity believed to assist a magician</gloss></term> (Lines 1—42; 43—195; 263—347). Between them are four recipes, three of which have no connection to the main part. The exact contents of the collected manuscript are as follows:

# I 1-12

mystery religions (1910. 327) were frequently brought into the discussion, and finally, the reference to Saint George in line 26 <note>originally: "Z. 26"</note> produced a small body of literature.1) With the active participation of Wilhelm Schubart [Sch], Adam Abt [A] collated the entire manuscript three times (1907, 1908, 1910). Karl Preisendanz [Pr] verified these results against the original (1919, 1924, 1926), revised Abt’s text, and edited several parts based on his own readings, for which the critical apparatus provides an accounting. Improvements and conjectures for the restoration of difficult and doubtful passages were provided by Richard Wünsch [Wü], Wilhelm Heraeus [Her], and Samson Eitrem [Eitr], who published the results of his collation in the *Contributions to the Berlin Magical Papyri* (1923); cf. also K. Preisendanz, *Spicilegium criticum*, Aegyptus 5, 1924, 21–26, where some restoration attempts are to be changed according to the latest comparison from 1926; see the critical apparatus. Theodor Hopfner, in his work *Greco-Egyptian Revelation Magic* <note>original title: "Griech.-ägypt. Offenbarungszauber" [Ho, OZ]</note>, Vol. 2, 1924, makes use of the Berlin papyri following the text editions of Parthey and Eitrem. The entire bibliography is collected in the report on the Greek Magical Papyri by K. Preisendanz, APF 8, 1926, 106–108; here also the history of P I and II is found. The critical contributions of Wilhelm Kroll [Kr] (Philol. LIV 1895, 564 ff.) and previously unpublished notes by Ulrich Wilcken in the personal copy of Parthey's edition (Berlin Papyrus Collection) are based on a new comparison of the original.

The physical appearance of the manuscript presents a picture typical of a document from late antiquity originating from the lower social classes, yet it was copied carefully on the whole. Thus, apart from the abbreviations customary in magical practice—which we may also assume were present in the source text—only very few unusual ones are found. Punctuation and reading marks are treated carelessly, though it remains undecided whether the inconsistency in placing or omitting them is the fault of our specific scribe. The *iota adscript* <note>a silent 'i' written after certain vowels in Greek</note> in dative and subjunctive forms and the *trema* <note>a dieresis mark (¨) placed over vowels</note> are also applied indiscriminately. A single apostrophe appears in the middle of a verse only in complete isolation.

And whenever you wish to perform a deed, speak the name alone into the air and say "Come!", and you will see him standing near you, and say to him: "Perform this task," and he does it immediately.

# I 273—317

The sea and stones shudder and the spirits <note>original: "daimones"</note> watch for the divine power of the magical signs <note>original: "charaktêrôn"; these are non-alphabetic, seal-like symbols used to command spiritual forces</note> which you are about to possess. For this is the greatest protection for the ritual, so that you may not be terrified.

The ritual is as follows: take an unpainted lamp and prepare it with a linen rag and rose oil or nard oil. After dressing yourself in a prophetic costume <note>this usually refers to wearing pure white linen garments like a priest</note>, hold an ebony rod in your left hand and the protective charm <note>original: "phylactêrion"</note> in your right—that is, the laurel branch. Have at hand the head of a wolf, so that you may place the lamp upon the wolf's head. Set up an unbaked altar <note>original: "bômon ômon"; an altar made of raw earth or unhewn stone rather than fired brick</note> near the head and the lamp to make an offering to the god, and immediately the divine spirit will enter.

The incense offering <note>original: "epithyma"</note> consists of a wolf's eye, storax, cinnamon, bdellium, and whatever is precious among spices. Perform a libation of wine, honey, milk, and rain water, and prepare seven flat cakes and seven round cakes. You must do all these things near the lamp, while dressed and abstaining from all defiling things—specifically from eating fish and from all sexual intercourse—so that you may bring the god into the greatest desire for you.

These are the names that you must write on the linen rag and use as a wick in the unpainted lamp: ‘Aberamenthoulerthaee, Lord Ethrenlyou Thnema Raibai; Aeminnae Barôther Rethôbab Eanimea.’ <note>These are "voces magicae," or "magical words," which often incorporate palindromes; "Aberamenthou" is a common title for the solar-creator god in these papyri</note> When you have completed all the aforementioned things, call out with the incantation:

‘Lord **Apollo**, come with the Healer <note>original: "Paiêoni"; an epithet of Apollo as a god of healing</note>; give me an answer, Lord, concerning the things I ask. Master, leave the Parnassian mountain and Delphic Pytho <note>the famous site of Apollo's oracle in Greece</note> when our sacred mouths speak unspoken things. First messenger of God, of Great Zeus <note>original: "Zênos megaloio"</note>, **Iao** <note>the Greek transliteration of the Hebrew name for God, YHWH</note>; and you who hold the celestial order, **Michael**; and you I call, **Gabriel**, the first-messenger; come from Olympus, **Abrasax**, you who rejoice in the East; may you come graciously, you who look down upon the West from the East, **Adonai**. <margin>Col. 5.</margin> Every nature trembles before you, father of the world, **Pakerbeth** <note>a powerful magical name often used to invoke a supreme, sometimes subterranean or solar, power</note>.

I adjure you by the head of God, which is Olympus; I adjure you by the seal of God, which is Vision; I adjure you by the right hand which you stretched over the world; I adjure you by the mixing bowl <note>original: "krêtêra"; a cosmic vessel, perhaps referring to the container of souls or the elements</note> of God that contains wealth; I adjure you by the eternal God and the **Aeon** <note>the personification of eternal time</note> of all; I adjure you by self-begotten Nature, the most powerful **Adonaios**; I adjure you by the setting and rising **Eloaios**; I adjure you by these holy and divine names, that they may send the divine spirit to me and fulfill the things I have in mind and in my heart. Hear me, blessed one, I call upon you, the ruler of heaven and earth, of chaos and Hades, where [the spirits] dwell... send this spirit <note>original: "daimona"</note>...’

# I 273—315

...through which all men are subject to you, and the sea and rocks shudder, and the spirits <note>original: "daimones"</note> guard themselves against the divine power of the magical signs <note>original: "charaktêrôn"; these are non-alphabetic, seal-like symbols used to command spiritual forces</note> which you will possess; for this is the greatest amulet of the spell; with it, fear <margin>275</margin> nothing.

The ritual procedure is as follows: take a lamp that is not coated with red lead <note>original: "mennig"; minium was often used to color pottery, but ritual purity often required "clean" or "unpainted" vessels</note>, and prepare it with a wick-strip of fine linen <note>original: "byssos"</note> and with rose oil or nard oil. Dress yourself in prophetic robes and hold an ebony staff in your left hand and the amulet in your right—that is, the <margin>280</margin> laurel branch. Have the head of a wolf ready so that you can place the lamp upon the wolf's head. Erect an altar of unbaked earth <note>raw, sun-dried clay rather than kiln-fired brick</note> near the head and the lamp, so that you may offer an incense sacrifice to the god upon it, and immediately the divine spirit will enter. The incense sacrifice consists of the eye of a wolf, gum resin, cinnamon, <margin>285</margin> bdellium <note>a fragrant oleo-gum-resin</note>, and whatever else is prized among spices. Make a libation of wine, honey, milk, and rainwater, and bake seven flat cakes and seven other sacrificial cakes. You shall do all this near the lamp, while clothed, abstaining from every impure thing, from eating fish, and <margin>290</margin> from all sexual intercourse, so that you may bring the god to the greatest desire for you. The names which you are to write on the linen strip and use as a wick in the unpainted lamp are as follows: (Magical formulas, palindromes). When <margin>295</margin> you have completed everything mentioned above, call upon the god with the magical hymn:

> ‘Ruler Apollo, come with Paieon <note>Apollo in his aspect as healer</note>, prophesy to me about what I desire, Lord! Ruler, leave the Parnassian mountain and the Delphic Pytho <note>the site of the famous Oracle of Delphi</note>, when our holy mouth prays the Unspeakable! First angel of God, of the <margin>300</margin> great Zeus, Iao <note>a Greek rendering of the Hebrew name for God, Yahweh</note>, and you I call, who holds the heavenly world, Michael; and you, Gabriel, first angel; hither from Olympus, Abrasax, you who take your joy at the rising sun, come graciously, you who look upon the setting from the rising, Adonai! All nature trembles before you, Father of the universe, Pakerbeth <note>a magical name often associated with power and the god Set</note>. I adjure also the head of God, which is the heaven; I <margin>305</margin> adjure also the seal of God, which is the prophetic vision; I adjure the right hand which you held over the universe; I adjure the cup of God, which contains wealth; I adjure the eternal God, the Aeon of all; I adjure nature, which became of itself, the strongest Adonaios; <margin>310</margin> I adjure the setting and rising Eloaios <note>derived from the Hebrew Elohim</note>; I adjure these holy and divine names, so that they may send me the divine spirit and it may complete what I have in my mind and in my heart. Hearken!’ <margin>315</margin>

Berlin P 5026. Acquired in the same way as P I. Papyrus roll <note>1. > “Blessed one, I call upon you, the leader of heaven and of earth, of Chaos and of Hades, where they dwell... Send this spirit <note>original: 'daimon'; in the ancient world, this was a neutral term for a supernatural being or lesser deity, not necessarily an evil 'demon'</note> to my holy incantations, so that by night, driven by commands under your compulsion, he—from whose remains <note>German: 'Hülle'—the 'shell' or 'shroud', likely referring to a piece of clothing or physical relic used to bind the spirit</note> this comes—may tell me whatever <margin>320</margin> I desire in my mind, and let him tell me the truth. Send him gently, mildly, and without him harboring any ill will against me. And you, too, do not be angry at my holy incantations, but protect me, so that my whole form may come back into the light of day unharmed; for you yourself ordained that these things should be learned among men. I call upon your name, which is of the same <margin>325</margin> numerical value <note>This refers to 'isopsephy', the practice of adding the numerical values of Greek letters to find hidden connections between words</note> as the Fates themselves <note>The Moirae: Clotho, Lachesis, and Atropos, who spin the threads of destiny</note>: (Magic Words).” And when he has entered, ask him about whatever you wish: about prophecy, about verse oracles, about <margin>330</margin> dream-sending, about dream-requesting, about dream-interpretation, about the sickbed <note>German: 'Krankenlager'; likely referring to 'incubation', the practice of sleeping in a sacred space to receive a healing vision or oracle</note>, and about everything that exists within magical experience. Drape a throne and an armchair with fine linen fabrics <note>German: 'Byssosstoffe'—a high-quality, costly linen used in ancient Egypt and the Mediterranean</note>, and you must stand there making an offering with the aforementioned incense. And when you wish to dismiss <margin>335</margin> the god after the inquiry, take the aforementioned ebony staff, which you hold in your left hand, over into the right, and take the laurel branch, which you hold in your right hand, over into the left, and extinguish the burning light, and use <margin>340</margin> the same incense offering while saying: “Be merciful to me, Primal Father, early-born, self-begotten. I adjure the fire that first appeared in the abyss; I adjure your power, which is the greatest of all; I <margin>345</margin> adjure him who destroys even into Hades: depart to your own ship and do not harm me, but be well-disposed toward me forever.”

---

The content is uniform; it concerns a **ritual procedure** <term>praxis: a magical action or deed</term> for obtaining prophecies. The text begins in the middle of a sequence <note>4</note>: lines 1–11 are the conclusion of a hexameter hymn and a prose **formula** <term>logos: the spoken words of a spell</term> to Apollo with a request for prophecy; 11–15 concern preparations before the **ritual procedure**, including necessary tools; 15–20 contain a recipe for a means of remembering the oracle; 20 to 34 describe the **performance** <term>poiesis: the act of making or doing the magic</term>, including execution instructions for incubation; 34–35 provide a recipe for the magical ink to be used; 35–40 provide a recipe for making a magical juice to be dripped into the right ear during the invocation; 40–42 provide a recipe for a means of remembering the oracle; 42–44 specify the time for the **invocation** <term>epiklesis: a formal calling upon a deity</term>; 45–64 involve compelling the gods for 5 days; 64–73 describe a **performance** in another manner; 73–80 describe the encounter with the god; 81–100 consist of a hexameter hymn to Apollo; 101–140 provide a prose **formula** to Apollo; 141–175 give execution instructions (**performance**) for the incense offering, the nature and decoration of the place of conjuration; 176–183 describe the dismissal of the god.

<note>4) In the margin at line 81, the note "Δ calling" <term>klesis: the 4th invocation</term> is recorded. If this is taken as the 4th "calling," then our text must have been preceded by two more invocations that are missing today.</note>

The manuscript contains only a few of the signs common in magical texts, but shows a much higher frequency of ending-abbreviations than P I does.

the system⁷); for the rest, it is no more free of slips⁸) and inconsistencies in the use of punctuation than the former.⁹) The iota adscript <note>A silent letter 'i' written next to long vowels in ancient Greek, often omitted in later periods</note> is completely absent, and the trema <note>marks like a diaeresis (¨) over a vowel</note> appears here as well with fairly regular consistency only in the magic words. In the representation of sounds, the same types of spelling confusions occur as in Papyrus I, so that the phonetic evidence also confirms the obvious conclusion drawn from the character of the script: that the chronological distance between the two papyri cannot be very great. They likely originate from one and the same library, to which perhaps one or another piece of the remaining magical papyri (see below regarding Papyrus V, VI, etc.) also belonged.

## II 17—47

To remember what is spoken, use this composition: take the herb **mugwort**, **heliotrope** <note>original: "heliopalion", likely a sun-stone or the heliotrope plant</note>, a **"breathing" stone** <note>likely a magnet or lodestone, believed to possess a "spirit" or life-force</note>, and the heart of a **hoopoe**, which is also called a **vulture-cock**; grind them all together, add enough **honey**, and smear your lips with it after first incensing your mouth with a lump of **frankincense**.

This is the ritual procedure: when you are about to go to sleep in the evening, clean your bedding with **donkey’s milk**, and holding **laurel branches** in your hands—the preparation of which is described below—recite the underlying invocation. Let your bed be on the ground, either upon clean **reeds** or a **mat**, and sleep on your right side on the ground and under the open sky. Perform the invocation without giving an answer to anyone; while calling out, sacrifice uncut **frankincense**, twelve right-turning **pine cones**, and two spotless **roosters**—one for the **Sun** and one for the **Moon**—on the first day, using a bronze or earthenware censer.

<margin>☥</margin> Write this character <note>original: "charaktēra", a magical symbol; the marginal sign ☥ resembles the Egyptian Ankh or a stylized letter</note> on the right, and sleep toward its vertical line. While praying, wear a **laurel wreath** made like this: take twelve sprigs of laurel and make a wreath from seven of them; hold the remaining five tied together in your right hand while praying, and sleep with it in the same position. Write with **myrrh-ink** <term>myrrh-ink: a specialized magical pigment made from soot, resin, and herbs</term>, as explained to you, on a **mother-of-pearl shell** <note>original: "pinnē", a large bivalve shell often used as a writing surface</note>... and hold it while praying with the laurel, [reciting] the names, the beginning of which is this: **BOLSOCH** and the following. The names written upon each leaf of the branch are: **UESSEMMIGADON ORTHO; BAUBO; NOERE; SOIRE; SOIRE SANKANTHARA; ERESCHIGAL** <note>the Sumerian goddess of the Underworld, frequently invoked in these spells</note>; **SANKISTE; DODEKAKISTE; AKROUROBORE; KODERE.** Write twelve names. The ink is as follows: having purely burned **myrrh**, the herb **cinquefoil** <note>original: "pentedaktylon", literally "five-fingered" herb</note>, and **mugwort**, grind them fine and use. Taking a **laurel branch**, **Ethiopian cumin**, and the herb **nightshade**, grind them together. Take water from a new well dug five months ago, or within five years, or whatever you find from the first day of its digging; bring it up in a ceramic vessel and put the ground ingredients into the water. Let it sit for only three nights, and while calling into your right ear, pour in a little. To help you remember, write the underlying character on a leaf of **cinquefoil** and keep it in your mouth while sleeping, having written it with **myrrh-ink**. The symbol is: <image-desc>A magical symbol resembling a stylized staff or a looped ligature, similar to a mercury symbol</image-desc> ☿. Begin the aforementioned invocation on the seventh day of the Moon, until he <note>the deity or spirit</note> hears you and you are joined with him. There are also other "compelling" rites <term>compelling rites: "epanagkoi," spells designed to force a deity to appear or obey</term>; they are all offered to the **Moon** after the first or second day. If, therefore, he does not appear, sacrifice the brain of a **black ram**; on the third day, the small hoof of the front right foot, the one at the ankle; on the fourth day, the brain of an **ibis**...

**Performance of the Rite:**
On the first day [burn] sheep's hooves, on the second day goat's hooves, on the third day wolf's hair or a knucklebone. <margin>145</margin> Use these incense-offerings for the other 3 days. On the seventh day, when he <note>the god</note> does not come, make a lamp-wick from a **cloth of one who died by violence** <note>Items associated with those who died prematurely were believed to have potent magical energy</note>, light the lamp with pure oil, and recite the preceding words, petitioning and entreating the god to come in goodwill. Let your place be holy and free from all defilement, and having purified yourself cleanly, begin the petition <margin>150</margin> of the god; for it is greatest and unsurpassable.

**The Ritual Action:** 
Taking pure clay, [plaster] the doorposts of the bedroom in which you are purifying yourself, and having thus plastered them, write these following things with a bronze stylus on the right doorpost. The things written are: <margin>155</margin> (See Plate I, Fig. 1.) "**Arsamōsi; noucha; .... ucha; 9,999 iē iē ia ia ie u iē** **Abrasax** <note>A common Gnostic name for the supreme deity</note> **lertheminōth**." And on the left doorpost similarly: (See Plate I, Fig. 1.) "**iōe; hōa; hiea; iaia; ieiaiēea; Harpon Knouphi** <note>The "Chnoubis" or "Kneph," an Egyptian lion-headed serpent deity</note> (the whole)." Above the door: <margin>160</margin> (See Plate I, Fig. 1.) "**aa ee Michael** <note>The Judeo-Christian Archangel Michael</note>; **ēia; euō; uae; euō; iae**." And below [the door], the **scarab beetle** <term>Kantharos</term><note>A beetle, symbolic of the Egyptian sun god Khepri</note>, as it is depicted, having smeared it with goat's blood, <column-break/> outside of the bedroom. <margin>Column 4</margin> Let the throne be pure, with a linen cloth above and a footstool below. And write on the throne, on the bottom parts: "**iē; iea iōau Damnameneus abrah; abraō abraōa**; Master of the Muses, be merciful..."

### Part III

The inventory of the Louvre Papyri gives under No. 2391 the indication that, besides the main piece of the papyrus, three further fragments are present. Until 1905 they had remained ignored; K. Wessely had only published the large piece in the *Memoirs of the Vienna Academy 36, 1888, 115—124 [139—148]* and in the *15th Annual Report of the State Gymnasium in Hernals, Vienna 1889, pp. 19—23*. In the year 1905, I succeeded—thanks to the kindness of Mr. C. Boreux—in seeing the fragments and having them photographed. When I undertook the first collation in the autumn of 1908 with the support of the Prussian Academy of Sciences in Berlin, and compared all the pieces once more in the autumn of 1910, the management of the Louvre Museum enabled me to use the papyrus undisturbed. I express my thanks to them and to the Academy of Sciences in Berlin here as well.

K. Preisendanz participated in the collation at the Louvre in October 1908 and, after the editorship of this edition passed to him, undertook some...

**166** Nothing can be seen of a correction of *phanēti* <note>appear</note> from *phanati* (as Pa suggested); the last two letters of the word disappear under a smudge. *hilaros* <note>cheerful/gracious</note> Eitrem (Parisian Magical Papyrus 34). The <term>Akephalos</term> <note>The "Headless One," a deity frequently invoked in these spells, often associated with Osiris or Typhon</note> (A. Delatte, Bull. Corr. Hell. 38, 1914, 215 f., K. Preisendanz, Akephalos 61 f.) bears 5 snake heads in place of a human head; in the right hand he holds an indistinct object—a flower according to Delatte—and in the left, which was originally drawn too high, a (laurel) branch or wreath. The Iota, which breaks the series of seven ε, is perhaps to be understood as an indication of the breastbone. **167** and **168**: Of the two words in each line, one stands to the right and one to the left of the torso of the Akephalos; below that, at the same height as the o-series on the torso, are the letters δα (*da*), perhaps *Damnamenous* <note>a magical name of power</note> was intended to be written here first. **169–173** stand to the right of the figure's left leg. **177** *peristeras* <note>of a pigeon</note> P. **178** *eipe* <note>say</note> P; the dots between the magical words are as in P. **181** *pros poi· epiork* <note>abbreviation for 'for the ritual adjuration'</note> P; *pros poiēsin epiorkismos* Pr. *chōri* <note>depart</note> P, corrected by Pa. *topous* <note>places</note> P. **182** *-leia*· *katalipsas* <note>leaving behind</note> P; *ischyn* <note>strength</note> P. **184** *akousin* <note>hearing</note> P; "they hear your strong power for you" Ho.

## III

Literature in Preisendanz, Bibliography of the Magic Papyri, Archive for Papyrus Research VIII 1926, 108/9: the abbreviations used there (166 f.) also apply to this edition.

The Papyrus of the Louvre No. 2391, named the Papyrus Mimaut¹⁾ after its former owner, was an <term>opisthographic roll</term> <note>a scroll written on both the front and back</note>, of which four larger pieces are preserved today under glass, in addition to a number of smaller fragments that are difficult to place. Based on the letter forms, the date of composition should not be set earlier than 300 AD. The height of the papyrus averages 27 cm. The width of the first piece, published by C. Wessely [We], measures 103 cm. That of the second averages 34.5 cm; the third 19.5 cm; the fourth 19 cm. The <term>uncial script</term> <note>a formal style of capital-letter writing</note> on both the front and back comes from the same hand; it is distributed across the width of the columns as follows:

The Old Coptic <note>A transitional stage of the Egyptian language written using the Greek alphabet with additional characters</note> texts of Papyrus Mimaut, lines 347 ff. and 633 ff., are previously unpublished. The relevant pages of the manuscript are very poorly preserved; the script is faded and rubbed away, and it is further interrupted by large gaps. The gain in text is therefore very small, and our knowledge of Old Coptic is only expanded by a few words.
->G. Möller†.<-

### III 1—64

Taking a cat, make it into an "Esies" <note>original: "Ἑσιῆν" (Hesiên). In Egyptian tradition, one who died by drowning was called a 'Hesi' and was believed to become a divine being or an 'Osiris.' This ritual deifies the animal to use its spirit as a messenger.</note> by putting its body into the water. In the water where you drown it, speak into its back. The prayer spoken during the drowning: "Come to me, you who possess the form of the Sun, the cat-faced god, and see your form which is being wronged by your adversaries, [Name] and [Name] <note>original: "τῶν δεῖνα" (tôn deina). This is a placeholder used in magical handbooks where the practitioner would insert the names of their enemies.</note>, so that you may pay them back and accomplish for me [the specific task], because I call upon you, sacred spirit. Be strong and powerful against your enemies, [Name] and [Name], for I adjure you by your names: **barbathiaō bain chōōōch niabōaitabrabra sesengen barpharargēs** <note>These are "voces magicae" or magical words of power; they are often untranslatable strings of sounds believed to command divine forces.</note>... **phreimi**, rouse yourself for me, cat-faced god, and perform [the specific task]." Add the usual concluding words.

Taking the cat, make three metal leaves <note>term: "lamnae" – thin plates of metal, usually lead or gold, inscribed with spells</note>: one for the anus, one for the mouth, and one for the throat. Write the prayer for the [task] onto clean papyrus with cinnabar <note>A bright red mineral used as ink in high-stakes rituals</note>; then draw the chariots, the drivers, the seats, and the attendants. Wrap this papyrus around the body of the cat and bury it. Light seven lamps on top of seven raw bricks and offer sacrifice to it, burning storax <note>A fragrant resin used as incense</note> and making yourself glad. Keep its body and guard it either in a tomb or in the place of burial... [drown/sink it] with colors... looking toward the East... saying: "Messenger... Earthly Sign... give security... Chthonic <note>term: "chthonic" – relating to the gods or spirits of the underworld</note> one, the race of horses... [the driver]... keep for me the spirit..."

"...the spirit of the place... and let [the task] be done for me now, now, quickly, quickly! Add the usual words. 

Then, taking the water from the drowning, sprinkle it in the stadium or in the place where you are working. The prayer to be spoken into the water from the drowning while you sprinkle is as follows:

> "I call upon you, mother of all humans, she who gathered together the limbs of Meliochos <note>Meliochos is a magical name often associated with the 'honeyed' or 'gentle' one, sometimes linked to Osiris or a chthonic protector</note> and Meliochos himself: **orobastria Neboutosoualēth**, catcher, corpse-mother, Hermes, Hekate, Hermes-Hekate **lēth amoum amoutermuyōr**. I adjure you, the spirit aroused in this place, and you, the spirit-filled daemon of the cat. Come to me on this day and from this very hour, and perform for me [the task]."

Add whatever usual words you wish. **chybbachych bachachych bachaxichych bazabachych baiachachych bazētophōth bain chōōch anibōōō chōche... phiochēn gēbrōchthō mysagauth cheōō... <note>The following section consists of scholarly philological notes regarding the Greek text transcription.</note>

The word "razors" (*xyron*) may be a scribal error for "ichnor" in Hesychius. Writing errors also appear in the following sections. Preisendanz suggests "komaros" (strawberry tree) based on Latin glossaries.
187—213: See Fahz, ARW 15, 1912, 409—421.
188: "autarki" in the papyrus. "of the date palm" and "magnetite" corrected by Preisendanz.
189: "having ground" corrected from "lioson."
191: "ounces" corrected.
193: "shaking" corrected from "seion." "Theion" means "god."
194: "conversation" corrected.
197: A curved flourished stroke appears in the papyrus. Below 197 stands the *paragraphos* <note>A mark used in ancient manuscripts to indicate a break in text</note>.
198: "in the mouths" and "keep back" corrected.
201: "streams of the rivers" suggested by Bruhn.
203: "in holes" suggested by Jacoby.
205: "Seimios" is a known deity; Sêmea may be a variant.
206: "Sun-beetle" (scarab) and "gold-haired" confirmed.
211: "fiery angel" and "Iao."
212: Compare P I 301, where Michael appears instead of Raphael.
213: "Be merciful" (Abrasax).
214: "And I call upon you, Airy Michael, for your help."

<meta>This page continues the ritual instructions from the previous section, shifting from general prayers for memory and solar association to a detailed litany of the twelve hours of the day. # III 501—553

What is your name? **First hour:** you have the form and shape of a **child-monkey**; you produce the <note>original: "elate"</note> **fir** tree, the <term>unseen stone<gloss>likely a dark or non-reflective mineral used in rituals</gloss></term>, the bird <unclear>e....aeno.....a</unclear>, and your name is **Phrouer**.

### 505
**Second hour:** you have the form of a **unicorn**, you produce the **persea tree** <note>an Egyptian evergreen tree sacred to Osiris and Thoth</note>, the **potter's stone**, the **alouchakos bird** <note>an unidentified species; some ancient commentaries link it to the kingfisher</note>, and on the earth, the **ichneumon** <note>the Egyptian mongoose, famous for hunting snakes</note>; your name is **Bazetophoth**.

**Third hour:** you have the form of a **cat**, you produce the **fig tree**, the **samouchos stone** <note>likely "psammouchos" or sandstone</note>, the **parrot**, and on the earth, the **frog**; your name is **Akrammachamarei** <note>a frequent "word of power" in magical texts, often associated with solar or protective deities</note>.

### 510

# III 554—591

# III 592—635

...with a heart uplifted to you, an unspoken name honored by the title of "God" and blessed by the holiness of God, who towards all beings and all things has displayed a fatherly benevolence, affection, friendship, and the sweetest activity <note>original: "energeia"</note>, having graciously granted us mind, speech, and knowledge: mind, so that we may perceive you; speech, so that we may call upon you; and knowledge, so that we may fully recognize you. 

We rejoice that you have shown yourself to us; we rejoice that, while we are yet in these created forms, you have deified us <note>original: "apetheosas"; the concept of 'theosis' or becoming god-like through divine knowledge</note> by the gift of your knowledge. There is but one act of gratitude from man toward you: to recognize your greatness. 

We have known you, O <gloss>life</gloss> of human life; we have known you, O womb of all knowledge; we have known you, O child-bearing womb in the father’s planting; we have known you, O eternal endurance of the conceiving father. Having worshiped such a Great Good as this, we have asked for no <insert>petition</insert> except this: that you be willing to keep us preserved in your knowledge, and that we do not stumble from this kind of life... <note>The text becomes fragmented here; it likely describes the transition from the prayer to the physical ritual</note>

---

<margin>Column XIX</margin> After sacrificing flour and ripened mulberries and unpressed sesame and an unbaked leaf-wrapped cake <note>A 'thrion' was a common ritual offering made of dough or ingredients wrapped in a fig leaf</note>, in which, by pouring beet juice, you will create your own shadow, so that it will serve you. 

Go at the sixth hour of the day toward the east in a deserted place, girded with a new ebony basket, and on your head a red sling-shaped headband, and on the right ear a hawk’s feather, and on the left, an ibis feather <note>These birds represent the Egyptian gods Horus and Thoth respectively</note>. Treading upon the spot, worship with hands outstretched and say this word: 

"Make my shadow serve me now, for I know your holy names and the signs and the symbols, and who you are hour by hour, and what your name is." 

Having said these things, say again the word mentioned above, and if it does not <note>i.e., if the shadow does not respond</note> listen, say: "I have spoken your holy names and your signs and your symbols. Therefore, Lord, make my shadow serve me." And at the seventh hour it will come to you, standing over against you, and you shall say to it: "Follow me everywhere." But see to it that it does not leave you. 

**[Magic words in Coptic and Greek]**

---

<note>The following is the ancient Latin translation of this same prayer, preserved in the 'Asclepius' (chapter 41), provided here for scholarly comparison.</note>

*Humanity’s only thanksgiving is the recognition of your majesty. We have known you, the greatest light sensible only by the intellect; we understand you, O true life of life; we have known you, O fertile pregnancy of all natures; we have known you, the eternal perseverance of all nature, which is most full through your conception. For in this whole prayer, worshiping the good of your goodness, we pray only for this: that you wish to keep us persevering in the love of your knowledge and that we never be separated from this kind of life.*

<meta>This page transitions from the ritual instructions of the previous sections to a formal codicological description of the physical manuscript known as the Great Paris Magical Papyrus (P IV). It describes the physical layout, construction, and scholarly history of the artifact.</meta>

<page-num>64</page-num>
<header>P IV</header>

->P IV<-

The so-called ‘Great Paris Magical Papyrus’: National Library <note>Bibliothèque Nationale</note>, Greek Supplement 574. A papyrus book of 36 leaves written on both sides. The pages not written upon are Folio 1 recto, 3 verso, 16, and 36 recto and verso; for this reason, in the *Catalogue of a collection of Egyptian antiquities by Mr. François Lenormant* (Paris, Maulde and Renou 1857), Papyrus IV is listed under No. 1073 as a **"manuscript on sheets of papyrus folded into a book, forming 33 leaves written on both sides."** <note>original French: "manuscrit sur feuilles de papyrus pliées en livre, formant 33 feuillets écrits de deux côtés."</note> The aforementioned number from the auction catalog is still pasted onto Folio 1 recto of the papyrus today, as it is also inventoried in the National Library as Anastasi No. 1073; however, the designation mentioned above is to be regarded as currently valid.

The maker of the book had 18 double-leaves at his disposal, which he folded in the middle into a book or booklet form and wrote upon continuously starting from 2 recto. The small Coptic piece on Leaf 1 verso may have been added later. This original form of the Papyrus can be determined even though the leaves have broken in the middle and thus fallen out of context: on Folio 6 verso, which is written along the long side because of a magical diagram, the anagrammatic part of the Iaeô-Logos <note>The "Word of Iaeô," a sacred name or formula based on the Hebrew name for God, Yahweh</note> is missing. This double-leaf broke apart at the time in such a way that the missing half of the aforementioned Logos ended up at the bottom of the inner longitudinal edge of the current Folio 31, where it can be clearly recognized upon close inspection. Therefore, the current pages 6 recto/verso once formed a continuous double-leaf with 31 recto/verso; compare my report in *Philologus* 68 (New Series 22), 1909, 575–577. Folio 1 recto/verso likely formed the cover of the book along with 36 recto/verso.

Size of the leaves: they vary between 30.5 cm and 27 cm in height, and 13 and 9.5 cm in width. Margins of various sizes have been left on all sides: Wessely, *Hernals Program* 1888/89 pp. 18–19.

C. Wessely, whom we thank for the first collation and edition of the papyrus (*Memoirs of the Vienna Academy* 36, 1888, 27 [4]–208 [184]), places the time of the scribe in the fourth century AD, "specifically more toward 300 than 400" (cited work 36 [12]). This¹) time is also when papyrus codices <note>An early form of a book made of bound sheets rather than a scroll</note> in general belong, the form of which shows only a single quire: W. Schubart, *The Book among the Greeks and Romans*, 1907, 117.

E. Miller had already published some hymn fragments from the papyrus without, however, specifying his source: *Miscellany of Greek Literature* <note>original French: "Mélanges de Littérature grecque"</note> 1868, 437–458; without stating the origin, he had a year earlier according to a copy—

***

1) See also *Vienna Studies* 8, 1886, 189: time of Tertullian <note>late 2nd/early 3rd century scholar</note>; place of origin: Lower Egypt, Herakleopolis. Albrecht Dieterich, *Mithras Liturgy* 2nd/3rd ed. 44: "The time of Diocletian <note>Roman Emperor, r. 284–305 AD</note> is therefore the point before which <note>original: "terminus ante quem"</note> the papyrus book must have been composed: in any case, the liturgy in this copy [lines 475–834] was written at the time of the high flowering of the Mithras cult." Ad. Deißmann, *Light from the Ancient East* 4th ed., 217–225, places the creation of lines 2993–3086 before the destruction of Jerusalem <note>70 AD</note>. Hadrian is referred to as King <note>original Greek: "Basileus"</note> in line 2448.

The report of 1857 was presented to the Academy of Inscriptions <note>original: "Académie des Inscriptions et Belles-Lettres," a French learned society</note> with a translation; see *Comptes Rendus* <note>proceedings of the Academy</note> 1867, new series 3, p. 93; compare 7, (1871, 352–357).

P IV was found in Thebes according to Lenormant's report:
*Mr. Anastasi, in his excavations at Thebes, had discovered the library of an Egyptian Gnostic from the second century.* <note>original French: "M. Anastasi, dans ses fouilles à Thèbes avait découvert la bibliothèque d’un gnostique égyptien du second siècle." Gnosticism was a diverse religious movement in late antiquity that emphasized secret knowledge.</note> To this library also belong the Leiden Magical Papyri, which the catalog also mentions: *the famous magical text in Demotic script [Pap. Leiden J 383] and two small Greek papyri folded in the form of books* <note>original French: "le fameux texte magique en écriture démotique... et deux petits papyrus grecs pliés en forme de livres"</note> [Pap. Leiden J 395 and the **Chemical Papyrus X**].

The text was compared against the original by W. Kroll for A. Dieterich for lines 475–834; Wessely gave supplements to his own edition in the *Hernals Program* 1888/89, pp. 12–19; the dimensions of the individual leaves <note>folios</note> are also recorded here [We²]; see further R. Novossadsky, *Palaeographical notes on the Greek magical papyrus of the National Library* <note>original Latin: "Ad papyrum magicam bibl. Par. nat. adnotationes palaeographicae"</note> (*Journal of the Russian Ministry of Public Enlightenment*, St. Petersburg 1895, 81–87), Kroll, *Philologus* 53, 46–428; 54, 562 f. A. Dieterich obtained photographic plates of the entire papyrus, which passed to the Heidelberg University Library after his death.

The papyrus was compared by me [Pr] <note>Karl Preisendanz, the editor</note> in October 1908 against the original in the National Library and using photographs, which I owe to the kindness of Mrs. Marie Dieterich. The deviation of my reading from those of Wessely and S. Eitrem, *The Greek Magical Papyri of Paris* <note>original French: "Les Papyrus magiques Grecs de Paris"</note> (1923), is not noted in every instance. Theodor Hopfner edited, explained, and translated numerous pieces of P IV in his *Revelation Magic* <note>original German: "Offenbarungszauber," a seminal work on ancient magic</note> [OZ] I 1921, II 1924 (Index in OZ II p. 167). Hopfner's textual emendations, taken from his manuscript intended for Wessely's *Studies in Palaeography* and provided to me for this edition, are marked in the critical apparatus as: Hopfner, handwritten.

R. Ganszyniec collated P IV in 1927 and made his results available for this edition during the correction phase.

Regarding the history of P IV and its textual-critical and religious-historical literature, see the bibliographic compilations by K. Preisendanz, *APF* <note>Archiv für Papyrusforschung</note> 8, 1926, 109–115. Photographs of individual leaves are found in A. Erman, *ÄZ* <note>Zeitschrift für Ägyptische Sprache</note> 21, 1883, plates III–V: sheets 2 recto/verso, 3 verso (Coptic); H. The Coptic portions <note>Coptica</note> of P IV were noticed early by Egyptologists, whom E. Miller (1871) said were lured by the "Gnostic cheese" <note>original French: "fromage gnostique"; a curious phrase used by Lenormant to describe the complex, perhaps "smelly" or dense, mixture of ideas in Gnostic texts</note> (so Lenormant, Catalog, No. 1073). Eugène Revillout autographed sheet 2 recto, 1–27 in the *Miscellanies of Egyptian and Assyrian Archaeology* <note>original French: "Mélanges d’Archéologie ég. et ass."</note> 3, 1876, Plate II, and transcribed sheet 2, 3 recto after the "Explanation of Plates" without commentary [Rev.]. Ad. Erman treated "the Egyptian incantations of the Great Paris Magical Papyrus," *ÄZ* 21, 1883, 89–109; here providing text, explanation, translation, and photographs (see above). H. Brugsch discovered in *ÄZ* 22, 1884, 18, the similarity of the Coptic beginning of P IV...

1) Regarding the explanation of this form, which is frozen in the third person and corresponds to the Ancient Egyptian <image-desc>Group of six small hieroglyphic and demotic characters meaning "he is praised"</image-desc> "he is praised," compare Möller, *Rhind Papyrus* page 86, Commentary No. 108. As Brugsch (*ÄZ* 22, 18) first established, the entire beginning is found, essentially identical in wording, in the *Demotic Magical Papyrus of Leiden and London* (DMP) 21, 2—3: <note>original Demotic: "šwë-të-f Wsjr pɜ pr-ʿɜ n tɜ Dwɜ.t pɜ nb n tɜ ks.t..."</note> 'Praise Osiris, the King of the Underworld, Lord of the Burial, whose head is in Thinis, while his foot is in Thebes, who gives oracles(?) in Abydos, in whom his ...... is in Pr-shilem, who is under the Nubian tree in Meroe.' 2) <term>3φΑ</term> <note>a Coptic/Greek word for "shadow"</note> explained by Brugsch as a constructed form of the word for "shadow" <note>Demotic: hjb.t</note>. Griffith agrees.

3) The word <term>περοτϥ</term> in the text should be corrected to <term>μεροτϥ</term> (Meroe) according to the Demotic text mentioned above. 4) <term>ϣΑϥ</term> <note>strong/mighty</note> is not attested as an adjective. The translation proposed by Griffith in *ÄZ* 38, 88, is supported by the gnostic gem Berlin 9864: "Michael most high, Gabriel most powerful." 5) Instead of <term>3ΑΝCΙΗCε</term>, read <term>3ΑΝCΗCε</term>. The place lies between Koptos and Dendera; see Brugsch, *Dict. géogr.* 659. The Demotic text (DMP, Column 21, 7) has "from the district of the Dog-Faces" <note>referring to Cynopolis, the city of the jackal-headed Anubis</note>. 6) <term>ΤΒΑΪΤωΤ</term> is likely to be explained, following Erman, by the old title of Anubis <image-desc>Hieroglyphic sign representing a jackal on a shrine</image-desc> 'he who is upon his mountain.' This designation was transferred to the god from the jackal, the sacred animal of Anubis, which tends to roam the boundary hills of the desert. A phonetic spelling <note>tp-dw-f</note>, which dismisses the interpretation 'he on the Horned Viper Mountain,' is found in Demotic (*Br. Thes.* 1001). 7) Lines 18/19 should be emended as follows: 'Praised is Anubis, the inhabitant of the district of Hansiêse, who dwells upon his mountain. Praised is Thôth, this twice-great, the Wise; praised are the gods, praised are the goddesses.' 8) The old title <image-desc>A small horizontal hieroglyphic/demotic sign</image-desc> <note>referring to Thoth as "Twice-Great"</note> see Erman, *ÄZ* 21, 95. 9) Hebrew <term>ארבע צבאות</term> <note>original Hebrew: "Arba Sabaoth"</note> where "Arba" (four) is equivalent to the four-letter name <note>Tetragrammaton: YHWH</note>, a circumlocution for "Lord of Hosts." <term>ΑΧΑΜ</term> is the Hebrew word for "the wise" <note>original: חכם</note>. ## IV 26–70

**Initiation, Nile, moon, rooster, scarab, ibis, hawk, horsehair**

Initiation: After purifying yourself for 7 days, come on the third day | of the moon to a place recently uncovered | by the Nile <note>This refers to the receding waters of the annual Nile flood, which left behind fertile "virgin" soil</note>, before anyone else has stepped on it or it has been surrounded (or <margin>30</margin> otherwise: flooded by the Nile). || Build a pyre on two bricks set on their edges, using olive wood—that is, vine-twigs—at the moment the sun is half-risen. Before the sun rises, circle | the altar; <margin>35</margin> but when the full solar | disk has emerged, cut off the head of a perfectly | white rooster <note>White animals were often preferred in "solar" or "celestial" magic as symbols of purity</note>, which you are holding in your left arm. Circle | the altar again before the sun rises [further]. Cut the rooster's throat while | holding it with your knees, so that no one else is holding | it. <margin>40</margin> Throw the head into the river; | catch the blood and drink it with your right hand. Place the rest of the body | on the burning altar, | and jump into the river. Immerse yourself | with the clothes you are wearing; <margin>45</margin> walk backward as you come out, change into | new clothes, and leave without looking back. After | this, take the gall of a long-eared owl and, using an ibis | feather, smear it on your eyes, | and you will be initiated. If you lack the [owl's] | gall, <margin>50</margin> use an ibis egg and a hawk's feather. || Pierce the egg and, after inserting the feather, break it [to mix the contents], | and anoint yourself in this way. |

After purifying yourself for 7 days before the moon becomes | full, <margin>55</margin> abstaining from living things and unboiled | foods, leave behind half of what you eat | during these days in a turquoise-colored <term>turquoise: the Greek "kallainos" refers to a blue-green color associated with the sky and water</term> vessel. | Abstain from wine while eating from this vessel. When the moon is full, | go to the eastern | parts of the city <margin>60</margin> or village, or to a solitary house in the fields, and throw || away the leftover portions. Then return quickly | to your place and lock | <margin>Folio 2 verso</margin> yourself in, || so that the spirit does not reach you first—for if you are caught first, you will be shut out by it. | Before you throw away the portions, fix a local reed about two | cubits <note>A cubit is roughly 18 inches or 45 centimeters</note> long in the ground, leaning it slightly, and hang || from it by the hair of a male horse a bull-shaped scarab beetle <margin>65</margin> <note>Likely the *Ateuchus sacer*, a dung beetle which the Egyptians associated with the sun-god Ra</note> | tied around the middle. Place under it a new | clay bowl and a new | lit lamp, so that the vapor | of the lamp reaches the scarab slightly. <meta>This page continues the specific ritual instructions from the Great Paris Magical Papyrus (PGM IV). ### IV 26—73

**Consecration: keep yourself pure** for 7 days beforehand and then, on the third day of the moon, go to a place recently cleansed by the Nile <note>This refers to land left behind by the receding floodwaters, considered ritually pure or "virgin" soil</note>, before anyone else has stepped into its <margin>30</margin> rinsing-circle (or otherwise: to a place washed by the Nile). Upon two bricks standing on their narrow sides, build a fire using olive wood—that is, from thin wood—when the sun is half-risen, after you have circled the altar before the sun rose; but once <margin>35</margin> the solar disk has fully emerged, cut off the head of a flawless, completely white rooster <note>White animals were associated with solar and celestial deities</note> which you [hold] in your left elbow; before the sun rises, circle the altar. Hold the rooster fast with your knees and decapitate it yourself, without anyone else holding <margin>40</margin> it. Throw the head into the river, catch the blood with your right hand, and drink it. Place the rest of the body on the burning altar and jump into the river; submerge yourself in the clothes you are wearing, then, stepping backward, climb onto the bank, change into <margin>45</margin> new clothes, and leave without turning around. Afterward, take the gall of a night-heron <note>original: "Nachtraben," likely referring to the Nycticorax or night-owl</note>, smear some of it onto your eyes using an ibis wing, and you will be consecrated. If you do not have a [night]-heron, use the egg of an ibis and a hawk’s wing: after you have pierced the egg <margin>50</margin> and inserted the wing-feather, break it after this smearing.

**Keep yourself pure** for 7 days before the moon becomes full by abstaining from bloody <note>meat</note> and uncooked foods. Of that which you eat, leave <margin>55</margin> half in equal portions for the following days in a vessel made of chrysolite <note>original: "Goldstein," a yellowish-green gemstone or gold-colored glass</note>, over which you also eat, and abstain from wine; when it has become a full moon, go to the eastern parts of the city or the village or the house, alone, and in the field throw away the leftover portions and <margin>60</margin> then return quickly to your place and lock yourself in, so that he <note>The spirit being summoned</note> does not get ahead of you. For if you are overtaken, you will be shut out by him. But before you throw out the food portions, fix a mature reed-staff of about two cubits into the earth, slightly inclined, and with <margin>65</margin> the hair of a male horse, tie a bull-shaped scarab <note>The scarab beetle was a symbol of the sun god Ra/Khepri; "bull-shaped" refers to specific horned varieties</note> to it, bound around the middle; place under it a new, burning light in a new earthen bowl, so that the breath of the light just reaches the scarab. Stand there undaunted after you have thrown the pieces away and have stepped inside and locked up. For the one summoned <margin>70</margin> will press you and, threatening and armed, will try to force you to release the scarab. But do not let yourself be confused and do not release it until he reveals [the matter] to you, and only then release it quickly. But if you eat daily during the purification period—

8) **TO CI NTO** also appears in Papyrus III line 679; thus the change to **no** ('the Great') suggested by Erman is to be rejected. Compare also DMP XVIII 14/15, where a 'dog-faced' entity is mentioned.

9) **noὐp ci nnoὐp** should probably be corrected to **nothp ci nothp**, following the common Egyptian magical claim "I am a Great One, son of a Great One" (e.g., Hieratic Magical Papyrus of Turin).

10) "The dog-faced (Anubis), who wears the gold crown" (DMP XVIII 14).

11) **CUUI** is the verb for "to know," constructed with **e** in classical Coptic.

12) Here, the name and mother's name of the person reciting the spell were to be inserted.

13) **πGỎΪ** (Line 1643 **ψoi**) is the Demotic *p' šj*, Hellenized as *Psais*, and translated into Greek as *Agathodaimon* (the Good Spirit).

14) Demotic *spš.t*, Hellenized as *Saipsis* or *Sepsis*, a title of goddesses. In the Rhind Papyrus, they are the female retinue of Osiris; at Philae, the goddess Isis.

15) **NABIN** is presumably an unknown goddess. Thoth's wife is usually Seshat or Maat, or sometimes Nephthys.

16) **KO** (Bull), ancient Egyptian *k’*, does not seem to be preserved in Coptic, but appears in Demotic glosses as *kö*. "Bull" is a common epithet for Egyptian gods; Thoth, for instance, is the "Bull of the West."

17) The word **xe** introduces indirect speech.
